thesis: With Bitcoin, a fleet of AI agents and cryptographic governance, anyone can do what used to need the permission of a corporation, bank, platform or state.

pillars.role: Move value: identity, entities, Bitcoin settlement, the economy that remembers need.
Get the work done: a captain over a fleet of agents, with verification and approval built in — and the people, commitments and spending the work runs on.
Coordinate without a coercive state: signed voting, transparent treasury, rules people can recount.

projects.name: loki
projects.what: Loki is an independent product for building and changing projects with AI agents. Start with a brief, create a real repository, build and deploy, then use project feedback to direct the next change. OrangeCat linking is optional; an OrangeCat account is not required to build in Loki.
projects.stack: Next.js 16 App Router · TypeScript strict · Tailwind 4 + ui-* design system (globals.css SSOT) · Drizzle ORM + PostgreSQL 17 (self-hosted Hetzner) · box-runner + Fleet Runner desktop (Electron, node-pty) · pgvector fleet-knowledge RAG (fastembed 384-dim) · Auth.js (GitHub/Google/X/email + OrangeCat OIDC)

identity.problem: Builders need a trustworthy command center for AI agents to manage multiple projects simultaneously
identity.solution: Loki provides a multi-user SaaS platform for commanding AI agent fleets across projects, with a focus on control, simplicity, and security
identity.mission: Direct the creation of everything you can imagine. Loki is the control plane for the age of autonomous creation: today one person commands a fleet of AI agents building software, tomorrow the same person commands fleets of robots building the physical world. Raw capability is no longer the constraint — human direction is. Every surface exists to raise the number of agents one operator can hold in their head and aim.
identity.vision: Leverage shifts from companies to individuals: a single builder, on their own machines and their own models, out-executes a team, and the only remaining bottleneck is their judgment about what to build. Deliberately open- and local-model capable, so creation is never gated behind closed frontier subscriptions. The commercial form — a high-retention SaaS for builders and small teams, with OrangeCat as the economic layer — follows from that goal rather than defining it.

changelog.done:
A bot can ask Loki. {#bots-ask-loki} One of the person's OrangeCat bots can ask Loki a question, as the person, over the signed OrangeCat rail (POST /api/orangecat/ask). Loki answers from their own projects, dispatches and pages; the turn is read-only, so a relayed question can never dispatch, approve or spend. A person whose OrangeCat identity is not linked to a Loki account is told the one step that links it.
Bots, beside Loki and Voice. {#bots-in-sidebar} The person's bots live on OrangeCat (the Cat, the fleet's specialists, the ones they made, and their group chats) and that list is where a bot's face, price and purse are. Loki now opens that one list from its own sidebar instead of growing a second one; a bot's work, when it has hands, runs here.

Two companions on OrangeCat (one arguing for Loki, one against), briefed on how Ask Loki works, agreed on three changes; this is them.
A build line only when you asked for one. {#build-line-held} Every answer used to be able to end with a bold project: task command, even "how much did we spend last week?". Now the line stays only when your message asked for direction (what next, what to build, propose, decide, a bare yes); otherwise it comes off the answer and the floating panel offers it under the answer as "Next build, if you want it" — a tap puts it in the box, sending is still yours. In the full Loki chat a "yes" after an answer that never offered a build no longer sends one.
The floating panel remembers, per project. {#panel-thread-per-project} Its transcript lives on your device, one thread per person and per project (and one for the fleet-wide pages). Leave project A for project B and you see B's thread, never A's questions as B's context; come back and A's is there, and the next ask sends it as history. Clear in the panel's header forgets the thread on this device.
Loki says what it is. {#advisor-boundary} Both of its system prompts now open the role with the same sentence: the advisory surface, not the executor — no Calendar access, no email, no direct change to the fleet, only proposals for the approval queue. The capability list said as much, but only on fallback turns and never as part of who Loki is.

The owner's launcher and its microphone are now one thing.
The microphone lives inside the launcher. {#mic-in-pill} "● Watching 🎤" is one pill: one outline, one place on the screen, moved by the same drag, long-press and menu, and folded away by Minimize together. It used to be a second round button drawn beside the launcher.
It is never alone. {#mic-never-alone} On Loki's own pages the launcher is the spiral in the top bar, and the microphone used to stay behind as a loose circle over the tab bar that could not be moved. Now the pill and the microphone appear together or not at all; talking from there is one tap on the spiral, then Talk.
The first look is whole. {#panel-first-look} A visitor's panel opened scrolled to its bottom with the greeting half cut under the header, and on a short phone the "Talk to Loki" card was sliced in two and the owner's way in was gone. It now opens at the top, the card and the sign-in line are shorter, and on short screens the sheet is taller and the suggestion chips step aside.

Every page was rebuilt to one bar, written down in docs/development/design-reset-2026-10.md: the way Claude, ChatGPT and Grok look on a phone.
Lists are rows, not boxes. {#rows} Projects, prompts, feedback, people, goals, habits, events, money, chats and sessions are lists of rows. Each row has a name, one grey line and one fact on the right, with no badges stacked under it and no card inside a card. Headings are sentence case, with no letter-spaced capitals and no explaining sentence under every title.
One action per page, in the same place. {#one-action} The page's one action is the round button at the top right, as "new chat" is in Claude. Everything else is in a row's "…" menu. Nothing sticks to the screen but the top bar, the bottom bar and the box you type in, so Projects no longer has a third of the screen pinned.
Projects read as names. {#project-names} A project with no title shows as words ("Murphys bar"), not its folder ("murphys-bar"), everywhere.
The bell counts what still needs you. {#bell-earlier} Old notifications fold under "Earlier" and no longer count, so a nudge from four weeks ago stops showing "9+". A repeat of an alert you forgot is raised again instead of being swallowed by the old one.
Home answers three questions. {#home-rows} What needs you, what is being built and what went quiet, each as rows with the reason in words ("Stopped: Claude hit its limit"), under the one box where work starts.
Send to terminal works for every project. {#send-any-project} A project with only a repository and no folder now starts or queues its agent, as every other send does, instead of failing with "no running agent". Run with Loki shows the answer as it is written, with Stop and Try again, and a prompt's blanks are never sent as {{project_name}}.
Missions and Settings finish the job. {#reset-last-pages} Missions is a search row and one row per project, and a mission's page is Objective, Next move, Roadmap, Latest handoff and Recent runs — progress still "reported", never verified. In Settings, Billing, Projects, Team and Privacy are rows too: projects move up and down from their menu (there was no way to drag on a phone), invitation links are copied, never shown as addresses, and the PIN forms open in a sheet.
Fixes found on the way. {#reset-fixes} An event without a deadline can be added again, events with a date and place are listed by that date, an ask with nobody on it can be given to someone, the /fleet filters open on a computer, the public home page's headline no longer waits for an animation to appear, a project's "What changed" is newest first, a request an agent received and then went silent on says "the agent went quiet" on the project page as Watch does, and Suggestions shows an avenue's best five instead of thirty "Put it online" rows.

Voice says why the studio voices are off, and how to turn them on. {#voice-studio-off} When Groq will not read aloud, the Voice page now says why in one line, with the link that fixes it: usually Groq's voice terms, accepted once at console.groq.com. Until then Loki reads with your phone's voice, and the page says so, instead of every voice quietly sounding the same.
Change Loki's voice by saying so. {#voice-change} "Use Troy", "switch voice" or "what voices are there" work while you listen, and questions about voice mode get true answers instead of advice about other apps. The status line reads as sentences ("Three runs failed on loki."), the music bed is pitched and loud enough for a phone speaker, End is no longer covered by the feedback button, and the voices are an even grid.
Watching says each thing once. {#watch-once} A page's findings are one card that updates in place, measured only after the page holds still, so "no main title" and "two main titles" no longer argue. A fix that did not finish says so, with a link to why. The header counts only what waits on you, and a saved note is never quoted cut off.
Prompts: one card per prompt, schedules in words. {#prompts-tidy} The same prompt saved twice opens the one you have, and extra copies go with one tap. Schedule a prompt as "every Monday at 10:00, Zurich time" instead of a cron line. Run asks for the project before it shows the prompt, both actions say what they do, and category tags are no longer orange.
A request goes to an agent the builder actually has. {#route-installed} When a project is set to an agent its builder does not have — Grok on the cloud builder, which runs Claude Code — Loki sends the request to one it does and says so on Watch it work, instead of starting nothing and showing "Grok is not installed on the cloud builder". A run that still stops for that reason offers the agent that is there as the one button, not "Try again", which would fail the same way.
Watch it work says a stop once, with the way forward beside it. {#watch-stopped} The reason and the buttons now sit together at the top of the card; the Loki message that repeated the reason and the "Stopped · 3 steps" line are gone, as are the pull-request, merge and live steps under a run that never started. An agent that never opened reads "could not start", not "stopped". Your request shows what you asked: the technical details a report carries for the agent sit behind "Dispatch details".
A partner you assign to a brief holds a seat on its project. {#builder-seat} Assign an approved partner to a website brief and, once the partner has signed in to Loki with the OrangeCat identity they connected, they are an editor on the brief's linked project and build in a private builder of their own, on their own engine. The seat follows the assignment and the project link and goes when either does; it is never a studio membership, so a partner sees one project and nothing else of yours.
A partner's fee is paid to the partner. {#builder-fee} With a delivery a partner can state a fee; Loki lists it as a service in the partner's own name on OrangeCat, with the partner's own sign-in, and the brief shows the link to pay it. The brief is marked paid by OrangeCat's settled payment, never by anyone's word, and both sides are told. Loki holds no money and takes no share.
Your requests on a shared project go to its owner. {#seat-suggests} Whether you are a Builder, a client or a viewer on someone else's project, what you ask for — on the project page in Loki or with Feedback on the site — is now a suggestion the owner decides on, and you are told when it ships. It used to build at once on the owner's subscription (a Builder's always, a client's up to a monthly allowance); nobody's request runs on another person's engine any more, and the "changes a month" setting is gone. A builder of your own on Loki's cloud is the next step on the roadmap.
A new account's first build runs on its own computer. A project with no stored builder used to ask for the cloud and be refused as "private" even with Fleet Runner connected; it now runs on the computer you connected, and a new project's folder is no longer written under the cloud builder's root for an account the cloud does not serve.
"Hosted runner" is offered only where it exists. It serves one account; everyone else saw it as a choice, could pick it, and queued work that was never claimed.
An agent on the cloud builder sees only its own environment. {#agent-env} It is born with what a shell needs, the engine key its account holds, and a token for the one repository it is working on. It used to inherit the builder's whole environment, database password and all.
The cloud builder asks Loki what to clone. {#runner-no-db} It no longer reads the database itself: it asks with its own token and gets its own account's projects and a token that account may use. One step from a builder with no database password at all.
A private builder per account. {#new-tenant} {#private-builder-flag} The operator switches it on for an account in System → Plans, and within a minute that account has its own builder on Loki's cloud: its own Linux user and home on the box, its own runner token, its own agent sign-ins, no database password, a memory and CPU ceiling of its own. Its Sessions page shows that builder; claude then /login signs in its own Claude account there. Nothing of the studio's — its GitHub organisation, its previews, the box's own folders — comes with it. Until now the cloud was the founder's alone, with an environment variable as the only other door.
Your own key builds, when you say so. {#your-engine} A key you added for Loki's chat can be marked "also for building" in Settings → AI; within a minute it reaches your private builder as Claude Code's, Codex's, Grok's or Gemini's own variable, and your builds run on it instead of a sign-in. A key stays chat-only until you say otherwise. The other way in is as before: start the agent in your Sessions and type /login.
Welcome builds, then your plan's, then your own. {#welcome-changes} An account with a private builder can choose to build on Loki's engine: three welcome builds to start, then the builds a month its plan includes (10 on Personal, 40 on Pro, 100 on Team), and past them its own sign-in or key. Every run records which engine paid for it, a dispatch past the last build is refused with the way forward instead of queued, and Loki's welcome spending stops for everyone at a cap in francs the owner set.
Capacity you can read. {#capacity-card} The System page shows how long work waited for a builder in the last day, per channel, and this month's builds, tokens and cost per account — beside what welcome builds cost against their cap. The numbers that decide when the box needs a bigger neighbour, read instead of guessed.

Answering a package update no longer makes it vanish. On Approvals, after you press Update, Not now or Stay on this version, the card now stays as a "Just done" line saying what Loki did (merged, merging when tests pass, snoozed until a date, or why it could not), with a link to the pull request. A new "Answered recently" list keeps the last two weeks of answers, with where each one stands now.

Several sessions at once, on a phone too. With more than one session open, the top of the Terminal is now a row of them, like a terminal's tabs: tap one to switch, swipe for more, tap the one you are in for its settings. + starts another session from the phone (it used to be desktop only).
A second session on the same project, side by side. Starting a project that already has a session now says so and offers "Start another session" or "Go to its session". The second one works in its own copy of the project, so the two agents never trip over each other's changes; it shows as "substrata 2". Starting the same project used to replace the running session.
Close a session from the phone. The session list in the settings sheet has a close button on each row (tap twice, so a stray tap never stops an agent).

Each tab says what its session is doing. A breathing dot while it works, amber when it is waiting on you, green when it has finished, grey when it is just open — on the phone's row of sessions and on the desktop strip alike.
Hear from the sessions you are not looking at. When another session finishes or starts waiting on you, one line says so ("orangecat needs you") with Open beside it. It goes away on its own, when you open that session, or with ×.

Chat does more, with less ceremony. From WhatsApp or Telegram you can now say "add dentist Friday 3pm" and it is booked without a second tap (events you ask for have no guests, so there is nothing to protect), ask "what's on this week", add a reminder or a note, and forward a screenshot, photo or voice note that implies one of those. Sending email stays off by design: Loki writes the draft, you send it. The chat skill now installs itself on the box when it changes, so it can no longer drift from the app.
Loki tells you when WhatsApp and the Telegram chat stop being read. The gateway behind them died on Oct 8 and nothing noticed for a week. Now a check every ten minutes raises an alert and one Telegram message when it is down, and another when it is back.
Turn on notifications on your phone. Settings → Notifications now has an "On this phone" card: turn them on, send yourself a test, turn them off. It says plainly when a browser cannot (on iPhone: add Loki to the Home Screen first) or has blocked them. Until today the server could send a push but no screen offered a phone the choice, so a new report on your site reached no device at all.
The server hands out its own push key. A phone used to subscribe against a key baked in at build time, which a build could lose or get stale; it now asks the server for the same key the server signs with, so the two cannot disagree.

A Packages page. Under Fleet, Packages lists every shared package the fleet registers (bitbaum/fleet registers/packages.json) with its latest version and, for each, how many of your projects use it and how many of those are behind. Search finds a package even with a letter wrong.
One page per package. It says what the package is, how to install it, where its code lives, and lists your projects that use it with the version each one is on — the ones behind first, saying by how much ("2 minor versions behind"), each linking to its project.
"Built from" on every project. The Story tab now shows the shared packages the project's repository depends on, at the version its lockfile actually installed, with the ones behind marked and linked to the package.
Nothing to set up in the projects. Loki reads each repository's package.json and lockfile from GitHub itself. It reads again when a page is opened and the last read is over six hours old, or when you press Refresh, and skips a repository whose code has not changed. A repository it cannot read is named, with the reason, instead of looking like it uses nothing. This is the read-only first step: choosing versions and rolling updates out come later.

Each project says how updates reach it. Under "Built from", one setting with three choices: Automatic (the default — an update merges itself once the project's tests pass), Ask me (each update waits for you on Approvals) and Stay on these versions (nothing updates until you change it back). The line under it says what will happen, and a change reaches the updates already open straight away, or within 15 minutes.
Breaking updates always ask. A new major version, or a new minor under 1.0, waits for you whatever the setting, because the project's code may need changes to take it.
Updates waiting for you are on Approvals. Each card says which project, which packages from which version to which, whether it is breaking, whether its checks pass, and links to the pull request. Update takes it (a breaking one is merged as soon as its checks pass), Not now hides it for a week, Stay on this version tells Dependabot to stop offering it.
You can see every update in flight. "Built from" and each package's page show an open update under the package it changes: waiting on tests, held for you, or ready.
Nothing new runs in the projects. The update pull requests are Dependabot's and the merging is the fleet's auto-merge, as before; Loki only puts a hold label on what should wait and takes off only the holds it put on — a hold someone added by hand on GitHub stays.

Before the first build, Loki says what the site will be built from. Under the start button, in plain words — "Your site will use sign-in, search, payments and email", how many other sites already run those parts, and that they are kept up to date automatically. It is read from what you wrote about the site; if it looks wrong, change the story — the build starts either way.
The first build wires those parts instead of writing them again. Its instructions name each shared package, how to install it, what to use it for and not to write that feature itself — so a bakery's search box, pick-up times and Twint payments come from the same packages every other site uses.
Client sites wear the client's look. For work done for a client, the build keeps the starter's design structure but replaces our colours and fonts with the client's, and does not install our design package.
What was planned stays visible. Under "Built from", a "Planned" line names the parts the build was planned with that are not in the code yet.
Whether the plan works is measured. Each first build records what it was planned with and, once its code has landed, what it actually installed.

Release from the package's page. Under "Unreleased", a package's page lists what changed since its last release, newest first, each change marked breaking, new or fix, and says which version that makes — a fix or a feature is the next small step, a breaking change the next big one (under 1.0, the middle number, which is what every project treats as breaking). Release vX.Y.Z asks once, then starts the package repository's own release step: it refuses unless the latest change passed its checks, builds, tags the version and writes the release notes. The panel follows it — releasing, released, or failed with a link to what happened — and the new version reaches every project through its usual updates.
Only the package's owner releases. That is whoever owns the Loki project that is the package's repository; for a package no project is, anyone whose GitHub access can write to it. Everyone else sees why not, and the way to connect GitHub when that is what is missing.
No dead ends. A repository without the release step says so and links the fleet's pull request that adds it (or the one-tap way to get one); a failing or still-running check links to it; nothing to release says so.
Rollout per version. For each recent version: how many of your projects are on it, have an update to it ready, waiting on tests, held or paused, or are behind with none yet. A version whose update fails its tests anywhere is flagged — "Red in 2 projects — their tests fail on v0.3.0" — with the projects and their pull requests.
Pause a release everywhere. The owner's Pause vX.Y.Z everywhere holds every open update to that version, in every project, whatever its setting, at once; those updates show "Paused by the package owner" on Approvals, the project and the package page. Resume takes off only the holds the pause added — a project on "Ask me" stays held, a hold someone put on by hand stays. An answer given on a paused update applies when it is resumed.

No download for an account that has the cloud builder. Opened on a second computer, Loki said Fleet Runner was not connected “on this computer” and offered one fix: download the desktop app. “This computer” is the one machine where your account’s desktop app runs, so from any other device that offer was a trap — and the account’s cloud builder was online the whole time. Now the card under a dispatch says “Run it in the cloud” (one tap, the work moves), the empty terminal says “Use the cloud builder”, and the Control banner says plainly that there is nothing to install. The download is offered only to accounts whose cloud builder is private.
The Terminal no longer says "start it" to a builder that is down. A deep link to a project with no session read “isn’t running on Cloud builder — start it, and it opens here” while the chip beside it said the cloud builder was offline. Now that screen says the builder is offline and what happens to the work, and the start offer waits for a builder that can take it.
The cloud builder's pulse is public. /api/health/builder answers 200 while the shared cloud builder is connected and 503 when it is not, so the box watchdog and the fleet sweep alert on it the way they already alert on a dead site. It was offline all night on 2026-10-11 and only a chip inside a signed-in page knew. Each deploy now prints the builder's state and its last journal lines into the CI log, and the feedback queue says “Cloud builder offline” instead of “Watch shows why” when that is the case.
The Mac download is not damaged. macOS says the app “is damaged and can’t be opened” because the build is not yet signed by Apple, and right-click → Open does not clear it. /download now leads with the .zip and one Terminal line that installs, clears the refusal and launches it. Signed builds need an Apple Developer account (USD 99 a year); the pipeline is ready for the certificate.
A Suggestions page. The "Build next" row on the Loki start screen only knew about code. The new page under Now reads every front Loki keeps records on — Build, Business, Goals, People, Money, Habits — and offers one thing to do per fact: the report nobody fixed, the delivery waiting on your yes, the goal due Friday at 40%, the subscription renewing Tuesday, the friend you have not spoken to in forty days, the twelve-day streak not checked off yet. Every card says which record it came from.
Two answers, no typing. "Do it" hands the ask to Loki, already written and already scoped to the project, or opens the one place only you can do it (checking off a habit, accepting a delivery). "Not now" puts it away for a month, with an undo. What you put away stays away on the start screen and on Control too.
It keeps score, from records. Taken this week, days in a row, taken in all — counted from the decisions you actually made, never estimated.
Private fronts stay private. People, Money and Habits are read only while your PIN zone is unlocked; locked, the page says so and offers the unlock.

Work sent to the cloud starts again. Since 22:25 UTC on 2026-10-11 the cloud builder stopped itself a few seconds after every start — 220 times — so every cloud dispatch waited in the queue. The form-filling window added to Fleet Runner that evening belongs to the desktop app, and the cloud builder, which runs the same code without a screen, tried to load it at start-up. It now loads only when a form arrives, which only happens on a computer. A new check fails the build if anything the cloud builder loads ever needs the desktop app again. Fleet Runner 0.8.42.

Search forgives a slip. ⌘K, People, Projects, Control's "Find project", Prompts, Goals, Events, chats, essays, the model store and the project pickers all matched the exact letters typed, so "lkoi" found nothing and "jonh" found nobody. Now one wrong, missing, doubled or swapped letter still finds the thing (two in long words), accents need not be typed ("zurich" finds Zürich), and "orange cat" finds OrangeCat.
The best match comes first in ⌘K, People, Prompts and the pickers, and ⌘K and the prompt picker mark the part of each result that matched. Lists with an order of their own — the sort you picked on Projects, Control and the model store, deadlines, recent chats, the goal tree — keep it; the search only narrows them.

Every agent Loki sends into a bitbaum repo is now told what already exists. Alongside the project's own profile, the dispatch carries the studio's rules: read fleet's AGENTS.md, STACK.md and SHARED.md first, start a new product from the fleet app template, use the shared packages (each with its one-line purpose and install command) instead of writing another health route, model call or set of security headers, keep the security bar, and count work as done only once it is merged, deployed and checked live.
The package list and the stack are read from bitbaum/fleet when the agent is sent, so they are never a copy kept in Loki. If GitHub is slow or down, the dispatch goes ahead with the last saved list.
Repositories outside the bitbaum org get nothing extra.

New sites start with accounts, three languages and strict security. Both ways Loki creates a site — "Make it happen" with the Next.js starter, and a new site on the box — now produce the same app: the bitbaum starter. People can create an account with a password, a sign-in link or a passkey (and with OrangeCat once the site is registered there), add two-factor sign-in, and use it in English, German or French. It ships with strict security headers, a health check, tests and the pipeline that deploys each change.
A new site gets its own database. Its accounts live in a database made for it on the server, with its secrets generated there and never shown.

"Build next" on the Loki start screen. Under "What are we working on?" there is now a row of things you could build, picked from your own records: visitor reports nobody has fixed, a project with code but no live site, the next step your last session left, a goal stuck at zero, an idea from your sticky notes, and needs people have posted on OrangeCat (the ones closest to what you already build come first). Each one names why it is there.
One tap starts the work. Tapping a suggestion for one of your projects sends it to an agent on that project. A new idea opens the new-project form already filled in, which leads straight into a kickoff. "Other ideas" shows the next set. With nothing set up yet, you get first builds that each end in something live: your own site, a page for your offer, a booking page.
Loki pushes to get it built. Ask "what should I build?" and Loki answers from the same list, recommends one thing and why, scopes the smallest first version, and ends with the exact line that starts it.

Visual fixes get a verdict too. A layout, a colour, a thing that overlapped: page text could not say whether the fix worked, so those were the ones still sent to your eyes. Now, when text cannot tell, Loki takes a phone-sized picture of the live page — scrolled to what the reporter pointed at — and asks a vision model the same question. The card says which it did: "Loki read /pricing" or "Loki looked at a picture of /pricing".
You see what Loki saw. When even the picture cannot settle it, the picture is on the card, under the reason, so "It worked / Not fixed" can usually be answered right there. Tap it for the whole page; it is also in every row's details.
A server with no browser says so on the card, in words, instead of a silent "cannot tell".

projects.name: orangecat

identity.problem: Economic participation is currently limited by gatekeepers, making it difficult for individuals and organizations to participate in the economy without restrictions.
identity.solution: OrangeCat provides an AI-native platform for universal economic participation, allowing users to manage their economic activity with full control and autonomy.
identity.mission: To enable universal economic participation by removing gatekeepers and allowing pseudonymous participation, with AI agents that can transact on behalf of users.
identity.vision: To become a platform where anyone can participate in the economy, regardless of identity or location, with full control over their economic activity.

Tracked public payment requests with confirmed amounts attributed to the correct entity.
Consistent share controls and link previews across public entity pages.
Open accounting: a wallet can publish its balance, its transactions, and the owner’s note on each one — for owners who turn it on.
A transparency score computed from what is observable in that ledger, never from what anyone claims about themselves.
Decide where money paid to you goes, in order — a share for taxes first, then a debt, rent or insurance — with each payment landing in the first wallet still behind. {#money-routes}
The tax line suggested from Solon's tax figures for your own commune, instead of a percentage you type.

Find what's on near you, on the page and through the Cat. {#events-nearby}
Times in the venue's own time zone, everywhere. {#event-time-zones}
Tickets with a QR code, checked in at the door. {#event-tickets}
A page for the place, listing what's on there, run by whoever runs the place. {#venue-pages}
The crew are people; the door crew check guests in. {#event-crew}
Pay the crew and refund tickets from the organizer's wallet, on the event's record. {#event-payouts}
Cover pictures: upload, find, generate, or the photo sent to the Cat. {#event-cover}
Guests without an account get a free ticket with just their name. {#event-rsvp-guests}
Guests without an account buy a paid ticket with their name and Bitcoin. {#event-paid-guests}
Tickets paid with Twint, bank or PayPal (waits on "More rails"). {#event-fiat-tickets}

roadmap.title: The investor portal {#investor-rooms}
roadmap.line: One link an investor can judge a project from, without a call or anyone's word: what it is, whether it is real and moving, why it exists, what it promised and delivered, the founder's story and the documents — generated from the product's own records wherever a system can count it. Questions in the room: a reader asks, the owner answers, everyone with a link sees the answer. {#room-questions}
Investor updates: a dated feed in the room. {#room-updates}
Documents uploaded to private storage, opened through expiring links. {#room-files}
The room shows the project's investment offering, when it has one. {#room-offering}
"Send Anna a link to the Heidi room" to the Cat. {#room-cat}
The studio room: one link for every product, with the machine's own numbers. {#room-studio}

changelog.done:
What a bot did stays in the thread. After you tap a “Do it?” card in a bot’s chat, the outcome (“Dentist is on the map. Open”, or the reason it did not go through) is now a line of that conversation: it is there after a reload, it is still there when a second card arrives, and the bot’s next answer knows it. Before, it lived in a slot above the box and left the screen with the next card.
The five bot demos are one button. A new Playwright spec walks orangecat.ch as a brand-new person: one door, the shelf and a real letter, a group with two specialists, an event proposed and created from a “Do it?” card, Loki asked twice, a routine set and stopped, and the API edges. The Live rehearsal workflow runs it on request, never on a schedule, and keeps every step’s screenshot. See docs/testing/live-rehearsal.md.
A “Do it?” card in a bot’s chat is finished when it ran, and a second one starts clean. A card whose action ran and failed kept its Confirm and Reject under the reason, so a tap would have run an action that was no longer pending; the reason is now the outcome line, like a success. A second card in the same thread showed the first one’s failure line inside it; it no longer does. And a bot that wrote only the proposal and no words left an empty bubble above the card; the card’s own description stands in, and a question to Loki is described as the question (“Ask Loki: …”), not “Execute Ask Loki”.
A bot keeps offering its hands. The second time you asked a bot for the same kind of thing in one chat, it could answer in words alone, with no “Do it?” card. Seen live: the second “Ask Loki” in a thread came back as “I can ask Loki for you.” and nothing to tap. The bot saw its own earlier offers as plain sentences, because the proposal is taken off before a reply is kept, and it copied them. It now remembers what it proposed, so a repeat ask gets a card like the first. And a first ask could come back as a code block instead of a card: “Here’s the query I’ll send to Loki:” over a bare {"question": …}, because the model was shown a template to fill and filled the wrong half of it. The instruction is now a worked example for a real action, and a block that names the fields but not the action is read as the one action those fields belong to, so the card still names it before any tap.
A “Do it?” card that fails says why, in words. When a confirmed action could not go through, the card showed “[object Object]” where the reason belonged. Seen live the first time a bot asked Loki for an account not yet linked to Loki: the sentence that names the one step was there, and the card lost it. It now shows the server’s own sentence; the same fix reaches the memory import and the interests list.
A bot can ask Loki for you. Ask a bot you made what is live, built or queued in your projects and it offers to ask Loki, the agent that builds and runs them, with a “Do it?” card; after the tap, Loki’s answer is the outcome line. Loki answers as you, from your own projects and pages, and the question can never dispatch, approve or spend anything: that stays with “send to Loki”, confirmed every time. If your OrangeCat account is not linked to Loki yet, the answer says the one step that links it.
A bot can write first. In a bot you made, Details has one row: “Writes first, every day”. Pick a time, say what it should be asked (“Good morning. What should I know or do today?” is the default), and every day at that time the bot writes in its own thread and you get a notification. It runs on your own key only; without one the row says so and offers the way to add it, and nothing is ever spent on a timer you did not choose.
Your own bots have hands. Ask a bot you made to set something up that OrangeCat can do (an event, a project, a product, a service, a wishlist, or handing a thing to Loki to build) and it answers with what it will do and a “Do it?” card, the Cat’s own. After the tap, an event’s outcome line now links to the event. Nothing exists until you tap; a bot never says a thing is done. The same permission check, the same consent row and the same standing grant as the Cat’s actions, so a bot can set nothing in motion that the Cat could not. Only your own bots, in their own chat, never in a group.

Companions are now Bots, and the Cat is the first row. The list at /companions/talk is called Bots, in the sidebar and on the page, and the Cat sits at the top of it: the one bot here that acts on OrangeCat (your things, your approvals), the same chat as its own page, so wanting something done never means knowing a second page. “Bot” is the word a messaging app already taught you; “companion” said friend where we meant worker.
A shelf of bots that come with a job. New bot opens on five ready to go: Letter Reader, Pitch Coach, Day Planner, Writing Partner and Study Buddy. One tap makes one, with its job under its name and a first line that says what to send it. A blank bot from a name, a shape and a colour is still there, under the shelf.
A new bot’s first line is there before you can type. It used to be a model’s greeting that arrived after you had already written, so the bot asked what it was for after being told. The first line is now written when the bot is made; a bot told its job in your first message takes it instead of asking again.
In a group chat, each bot keeps to its job. A question with a medical half and a legal half, sent to nobody by name, used to be answered whole by whichever bot spoke first. Now the question goes to each bot whose job a part of it is, a bot hands another’s part over with an @ instead of answering in its place, and the floor passes to a bot whose part is still open.
The New bot sheet fits the screen. On a phone and on a short desktop window its title, close button and first row were cut off above the top edge; a sheet taller than the screen now scrolls inside it, with its head in view (chatkit 0.21.5).
A row’s last line is plain words. A preview read “What the clause says” with the asterisks; the markdown is gone from the list.
The group router answers for each bot. It used to be asked to name “the one or two best placed” and named one; it is now asked, bot by bot, whether a part of the message is that bot’s job, so a question with a medical half and a legal half reaches both.
When the day’s free messages are spent, the chat says so. The eleventh message of the day used to come back as “That did not go through. Try again.”, which was not true and led nowhere. The chat now shows the real line (the daily limit, and that your own key lifts it) with a button to your AI settings.
No bot makes up a number. Every bot’s definition now says so: where it needs a figure, a name, a date or a source it does not have, it writes [X] and says what to fill in. Found when a pitch rewrite opened with a statistic from nowhere.
A companion keeps the job you give it. Your first answer to a new companion’s “What should I help you with most?” now becomes the companion itself: its definition and the line under its name, not a memory that might not be there. It holds in every conversation, every group chat and every clone, and the question is never asked again. Found by putting two companions on a real job in a group chat: both had been given their jobs a minute earlier and both asked again.
A model that answers with nothing no longer ends the turn. On the platform chain an empty answer (a reasoning model that spent its budget thinking) now passes to the next link instead of coming back as a blank. A new companion may also answer at length: its cap is 2,048 tokens, not the table’s 1,000, which cut a three-part proposal mid-sentence.
A member that answers with nothing shows as a failed line, with Retry, never as an empty bubble.

Your companions live in one place, and they can talk to each other. /companions/talk is now the home for every companion you made or talk to, your group chats and the fleet's own bots (Diplodoctor for a medical report, Causius for a legal letter), in one list with the last line and when, the chat beside it on a wide screen and in its place on a phone. "+" offers New companion and New group chat. In a group chat of two to six, the companions you address with @ answer in turn, hand the floor to each other with an @, and every line says who said it; a round stops after six lines so nobody talks forever.
A companion in a minute. New companion asks for a name, a shape and a colour, nothing else; it asks what you need it for in its first message and remembers your answer. The full form is still on the edit page.
A chat with a fleet bot stays in your browser. Diplodoctor and Causius keep nothing, and neither do we.
“Diplodoctor: …” and “Causius, your turn” address them too. A name that opens a sentence, followed by a colon or a comma, hands the floor like an @ does, for you and for the bots. A bot that labels its own line with its name no longer shows the label; the thread already says who spoke.
A group chat is a conversation, not a staging. A companion brings what it knows about you (the job you gave it) into the room, so it does not ask again. When a bot starts writing another member’s lines, its line is cut where the other voice begins and that member answers for itself. And when a line answers nobody by name but the work you asked for is not done (a discussion unfinished, a question open, a disagreement standing), the floor passes to the right member, up to the round’s six lines.
In a group chat, Diplodoctor and Causius know who else is in the room. Each fleet bot gets the room (the others’ names and jobs, speak as yourself only, @ a companion once when you need it) with every request, so a bot no longer writes another member’s line for it.
Attach a photo, a PDF or a text file in any companions chat. The paperclip is the Cat’s: Camera · Photos · Files, the same limits, the same PDF reading. A companion sees the photo and reads the file, in a one-to-one chat and in a group chat; Diplodoctor and Causius read an attached document (a photo stays on their own sites, and the box says so).
The fleet’s agents wear their own marks. Diplodoctor and Causius show the face their own site shows, not one made up here; the first screen is one line and a way into the product, and it no longer sits under the header.
Companions is in the sidebar, beside Cat. In a group chat every line reads "Name · job", the box says which group you are writing to, and the details sheet lists the members with Add member as the last row and Remove on each while the group keeps two.
Partners are now called builders. The independent people bitbaum's studio approves on their shipped work, who watch over projects built with Loki at their own price, are builders: "Builders" in the footer, orangecat.ch/builders, and bitbaum's builders (https://bitbaum.orangecat.ch/builders/). "Partner" read like a share in the business, which it never was. orangecat.ch/partners still works and lands in the same place.

Your things go in from the same sheet as photos, and stay on your message. The paperclip now opens one sheet: Camera · Photos · Files, then One of your things, Context documents and Connections & keys — there is no second button beside it. A listing or note you add shows on your message the moment you send it, not only after a reload. When a turn fails, it says why in its own bubble, and Retry sends its photos again. Links to create something and the "sharper on a frontier model" note show under the latest answer only. A sentence handed to the Cat from the door, the search palette or an "ask about this" link is sent in a new chat as before.
The Cat chat is the fleet's chat app. The list of your chats now has search, Today / Yesterday / Earlier, and Rename beside Delete; on a phone it opens from the left, on a wide screen it stays beside the chat. Reloading the page reopens the chat you were in instead of a blank one. You can type your next message while the Cat is still answering — it waits above the box and goes when the answer lands. Photos and files attach from Camera · Photos · Files and show in your message after it is sent; your own listings and notes are under the box's "Your things". Temporary chat is in the "…" menu, and still leaves nothing behind.

A request for CHF 20 stays CHF 20. When you ask someone for money in a currency, the request is held in that currency until it is paid. The person asked sees "CHF 20.00" in their notification and in the list, and the pay page opens on what CHF 20 comes to in Bitcoin that day, not on the Bitcoin figure frozen into the link when you asked. The request turns Paid when the payment covers the ask at that day's rate, with two percent of room for the rate moving between the invoice and the payment. Requests made in BTC work as before. If we have no rate for your currency, the request is not sent, and the screen says so rather than guessing a figure.

Request validation uses patched parsers. Updated runtime validation and compressed-body parsing dependencies to close denial-of-service advisories.
Pay from your own wallet in one tap. If you are signed in with a wallet connected, a pay link now offers Pay from my wallet: it pays the invoice without leaving the page, and the receipt appears as before — the request turns Paid, and the person who was paid is told it was you by name. Paying from a wallet this way is the one case where they see who paid; scanning the code with any other wallet stays anonymous, and the page says so under the button. If your wallet says no, the code is still there to pay from another wallet. If it times out, the page keeps watching the same invoice and offers no second payment: Lightning has no cancel, so a retry could pay twice.
Integrations load the right identities and recover from errors. Acts as reads the actual API response, failed loads offer Retry, stale identities cannot create credentials, and each app stays locked during its own pending permission change. Creation forms expand on demand, with clear Read/Write choices and larger touch rows.
Receive tells you when you were paid. Show your code, and when the payment lands the screen turns into a receipt — the amount in your currency, who paid and what for when that is known — with a Done to return to the code. It appears as soon as the payment is confirmed: within seconds while the payer's page stays open, and when the background check sees it if they close it. Payments sent straight to you@orangecat.ch are not seen by us and do not appear here.
Mobile sheets keep content scrolling separate from dismissal. Swipe the handle to close; scrolling the body no longer dismisses the sheet. Cancelled gestures reset, and simultaneous sheets have distinct accessible names.
Cancelling a confirmation returns keyboard focus. Shared confirmation dialogs remember their actual opener, including inbox delete buttons that are not Radix dialog triggers.
The money screens are set like they matter. The amount is now a figure: the number large and centred, the currency small beside it, what actually moves (the Bitcoin amount) quietly beneath — on Send, Request, the pay page, the receipt and every request row. Receive is a poster rather than a box in a box: your name, then the code, with the Cat in its middle (it still scans), then Copy link · Share. Every way to be paid carries a round mark, and the Bitcoin one is the only orange. A confirmation draws its ring and tick instead of dropping in. People with no name show their handle once instead of twice. Underneath: stacked lines no longer carry a hidden 12px gap.
Bookings distinguish an empty list from a failed load. Retry restores a failed request, view choices share one control, and history filters cannot hide incoming or confirmed bookings.
Cat’s editor directions open the editor. Known creation paths and named editor suggestions become direct links, including answers that show a path as plain text. Duplicate editor suggestions collapse into one action.
Ask Cat without an automatic upgrade pitch. Writing, creating or using another language no longer triggers a model promotion just because of keywords. Model choices remain available in AI settings.
Install metadata points to supported app resources. The manifest no longer advertises missing screenshots, dead payment-protocol pages or an unimplemented file-opening flow. Generated icon files stay unchanged, and duplicate metadata has been removed.
Short-post drafts keep your latest words. Closing the composer saves immediately. Drafts are separated by account and reply, storage errors offer Retry save, and older device-wide writing requires consent before private recovery.
A request you paid now says Paid. Until now a request stayed Pending, with a Pay button, for both people — even after the money had moved, which invited paying twice. The pay link from a request now names it, so the payment answers it: the request turns Paid, the person who asked is told who paid and for what, and opening the old link shows "This request is already paid" instead of an empty form. A payment smaller than the ask leaves it open.
A send that times out no longer invites a second payment. Lightning has no cancel, so a timeout can still go through. Send used to drop you back on the filled-in form with the button live; it now stops on "Not confirmed yet", asks you to check your wallet, and starts clean.
Send says it before you type an amount. Your own name now reads "That's you", and someone who can only be paid on-chain gets a link to their pay page instead of a refusal after the review step.
Dead ends say why, and offer a person-to-person way forward. The pay page for someone with no wallet now reads the same as Send, with the same one-line way to message them.
Notifications count in your currency. "Lena asked you for CHF 20.00" and "You were paid CHF 5.00" instead of BTC decimals; a request you asked for tells you who paid it.
Ask Cat from Home with the same composer as chat. Type or dictate your intent, then open Cat with your words intact. Home no longer opens the keyboard automatically; chat actions follow the app’s monochrome button style.
Task filters apply what you choose. Type and archived choices now reach the API. Filter controls have labels, phone actions keep their names, tasks open with keyboard-accessible links, and a failed list offers Retry.

A person who cannot receive Bitcoin is no longer a dead end on Send. The note now says why — they have not added a Bitcoin wallet, so a payment has nowhere to land — and under it, one line: "Message Marco to suggest adding one". It opens your conversation with them with a short, friendly message already written, including a link that shows how to get a wallet. Nothing is sent until you press send, and you can change the words.
Keep more than one piece of writing in progress. New draft preserves your current article, device drafts stay with the signed-in account, and the draft limit no longer silently removes older writing. Recover older unowned device drafts only when they are yours; failed saves and deletions keep your writing available for retry.
Notification settings explain what you change. Each toggle names its email category, saves cannot overwrite one another in flight, and a failed initial load offers Retry. Cat instructions use a labeled field that stays readable on phones.
Cat can distinguish app help from personal data. Writing destinations come from the Create catalog and count as verified application facts even for a new account. Answer repair preserves valid editor links while retaining checks against invented claims about your records.
Draft switching protects unsaved writing. If device storage cannot save, your current draft stays open for retry. Clearing a draft also clears its saved text instead of restoring an older version after navigation.
Cat's editor suggestions open the editor. Recognized Open shortcuts go directly to real creation pages. Automatic memory skips one-off writing requests and routine app praise, checks duplicates within each batch, and respects unavailable memory controls. Several new notes stay compact; failed Undo is visible and memories have a direct review link.
Messages work with keyboard and touch. New Message closes with Escape and restores focus, the Unread filter says what it shows, and conversation search tolerates typing slips. Failed inquiries offer Retry. The composer clears the mobile bar without a second blank band; shared fields are readable on phones and required textareas enforce validation. A slow session-sync request no longer sends a signed-in reader back to sign-in.
Your articles remain yours to open and edit. Private article reads, edit/delete controls and profile article lists now use the same author identity as publishing. Followers-only articles check the follow relationship. Writing uses a focused application workspace; published readers remain public.
Tell Cat when an answer missed. Under every answer, beside Copy and Listen, a thumb up and a thumb down. The thumb down asks why in one tap — wrong, gave up instead of looking, too vague, misread, too long, hard to read — and takes a few words. What you say stays with the conversation, and each night the fleet's reviewer reads the day's conversations beside what Cat was actually able to do, so a wall or a wrong tool is found and fixed without you having to report it twice.
Profile setup is a choice. Wallet connection is suggested when you need payments, without a Critical badge. Setup controls fit smaller screens, and Show more actually reveals the remaining tasks. Generated identifiers stay out of the welcome heading. The mobile menu and Create sheet support keyboard dismissal and focus management.
Posts require your own signed-in identity. The older post writer now checks authorship inside the database function, including requests made directly to its API.
Request and Send start from your people. Under From and To, before you type, the people you follow, who follow you and whoever you have asked or been asked by — each row saying why they are there. From the first letter the list narrows, and every account with a handle is found, not only the ones that wrote a bio: the person you followed this morning was invisible to the shared search, which lists a profile only once it has said something about itself. While the list has rows, "nobody goes by @me" stays quiet.
Receive is your code, nothing else. "Add an amount" is gone from under the QR: the code says who you are, the payer types what they owe on the page it opens, and a figure you want from a particular person is a Request. The link under the code no longer wraps a raw BTC decimal across two lines.
Wallets: the in-app Receive button is monochrome like every in-app action, the page is called Wallets, and every wallet carries the same mark instead of an emoji.
Home is easier to read on a phone. Long suggestion and project names wrap, recent activity shares the dashboard's section layout, and the Cat tab replaces the floating button on mobile pages with a bottom bar. Project updates keep their source and full text behind “Read update”. Draft counts stay current; status copy describes Cat approvals rather than claiming nothing is waiting. Failed suggestion dismissals are reported, and cached suggestions no longer propose listing bitcoin as a rentable item.
Request and Send find the person as you type. The field used to resolve an exact username after a pause, so "m" produced "Nobody goes by @m". Now a list of people appears under the field from the same typo-tolerant search as ⌘K; tap one and the handle is filled in.
Writing starts with your words. The article editor leads with the title and body, with AI tools and cover details available when needed. Drafts flush before leaving the page, and failed local saves are visible. The article list keeps its Write label on phones.
One Cat mark across the app. Cat's launcher, navigation and chat now use the same mark as the header. Install icons are versioned from that mark, and the app refreshes brand files instead of keeping old images indefinitely. The mobile Create button offers both Article and Post.
Write an article from Create. Article appears alongside Post in the header menu, mobile sheet and Create page. Cat links directly to the article editor without requiring a project. The header menu now supports keyboard navigation and keeps its choices within the available screen space.

One orange. The accent is now Bitcoin orange. It means two things and only two: Bitcoin, and the one button that brings someone in.
An invoice on a phone leads with Open in wallet. A phone cannot scan its own screen, so the code moved behind "Show the code to scan" on phones and stays first on a laptop. One line says what the invoice is and how long it lasts.
Zcash instead of Monero as the second self-custody way to be paid.
The code scanner's "camera declined" card now says exactly where to allow it and has Try again beside Paste instead. Request and Send no longer say "nobody goes by @m" after one letter.
A way to be paid can be shared only when asked. A Twint or Swish row is a phone number, and the first version printed it on your public pay page. Now each way is either on your page or shared on request: the page shows the rail by name, a payer taps Ask and it opens a message to you, and the number never reaches the page at all. Phone-number rails default to on request. Before you save any way, the sheet says what a payer learns — "your name and your phone number" for Twint, "only @you" for Bitcoin — because every fiat app shows the payer your registered name, whatever OrangeCat does.
Ways to be paid from everywhere. Pix, UPI, M-Pesa, Alipay, WeChat Pay, PayNow, Swish, MobilePay, Bizum, Wero, Tikkie, Zelle and Interac e-Transfer join the list, grouped by where people use them, worldwide first. Each knows what you type (a UPI ID, a Pix key) and the amount travels into a link only in a currency that rail counts in.
Receive opens on a code people can scan. The QR slot in the bottom bar now shows a QR of your pay link, with your name on it, the link under it, and Copy link · Share as two equal buttons. Add an amount and the code and the link carry it. Under the code, every way you are paid, in one list: Bitcoin first (your name@orangecat.ch and the wallet it lands in), then any other app you add.
You can be paid in whatever people have. Add Twint, PayPal, Revolut, Cash App, Venmo, Wise, a bank account or any link as a way to be paid. Your pay page shows each one with the one thing it supports: a tap that opens the app with the amount filled in, or the handle to copy. These settle in those apps, straight to you; OrangeCat shows them and never holds the money. A page with no Bitcoin wallet but a Twint number is still a page someone can pay.
Send reads what you give it. One field takes a username, a Lightning address, an invoice, or a code from the camera — someone's Receive QR included, with the amount they asked for already filled in. The "To a person / Paste invoice" switch is gone; the text says which it is.

An app you sign into with OrangeCat can list a service in your name. It asks for that on the consent screen, marked as acting for you, like posting to your wall. A service listed through an app can be live at once instead of waiting as a draft, and when a client pays for it, Loki hears about it the way it already hears about project funding. This is how a builder booked through Loki gets paid: the fee is a service in the builder's own name, paid to the builder's own wallet, and the booking is marked paid from the payment itself.
A product, service, cause or document created for a group now belongs to the group. The API layer worked out who the thing was for, but these four create paths rebuilt their row and dropped that, so the row fell to the person who clicked. The check that pins the carrier on every create path saw past them because of a type argument; it no longer does.

One wrong letter no longer loses anything. Type cqto and you get Cato; lki finds Loki, bitcon finds Bitcoin, farmhuose finds Farmhouse, setings takes you to Settings. Every word may carry one slip from four letters and two from eight — a wrong key, a missing, doubled or swapped letter — and a short word that matches nothing may still be a longer name with a letter dropped. Exact names still come first, and what matched is marked even when it was misspelled. When nothing matches, Discover asks "Did you mean …?" with the closest real name.
Discover is a page you can finish. One search field and one row of kinds — each with how many there are — then what was just listed, then a row of each kind: projects, things to buy, services, events, causes, people. Every card has the same parts in the same places: picture or initial, what kind of thing it is, the name, two lines, and the one fact that matters (the price, the goal, the date and place). It ends with the count of everything here and a way to list yours. It used to open on fifteen tabs and a sidebar of filters, several of which never filtered anything.
Search finds what you meant. Type two letters and it finds names that start with them ("lo" finds Loki); get a letter wrong and it still finds it ("lokii", "bitcon"); accents don't matter ("zurich" finds Zürich). Exact and leading title matches come first. The words you typed are marked in every result.
A project with nothing raised yet says "Be the first to back this" on profiles, instead of a bold "No funds yet".
"What it solves" asks which problem is yours instead of listing all twelve. Pick For you or For everyone, then the problem that sounds like you; its answer and the one thing to do next appear beside it (under it, on a phone). The same twelve answers, a sixth of the reading at a time.
Signing in looks like the front page. The same mark drawing itself, the same depth behind it.
A project without a picture shows its initial, not a generic target icon, on profiles.
The thing you typed whole comes before the longer thing that starts with it. Searching "lki" put "Loki — Capability Layer for a Permissionless Economy" above the project named Loki; a name matched end to end now ranks first. And in the quick search, a page you misspelled ("setings") comes before a listing that only mentions the word somewhere in its description, so Enter opens Settings.
Settings → Usage only says what it knows. The free-pool card said "nothing used yet — full allowance available" when it simply had no reading — next to a counter showing you had already sent a message. It now says "No reading yet", shows when each number was read, and says "Used up" when a provider has refused for the day, even if its headers still look healthy. Plans that can't be bought yet say "Not open yet" instead of "Activating", the Cat Credits card no longer points you to a top-up that is closed, and the explanations no longer credit Supporters who can't exist yet or give a reason for the midnight-UTC reset that isn't true.
A shared project link shows the project. It used to preview as the creator's face — Loki's page showed Cato — or as a broken image when the creator had none. Now the card carries the project's own mark or initial, its name, one line on what it is, and who is behind it.
Discover's people are people who have shown up. On the day the new Discover went live, its "Just listed" row was four untouched accounts with generated names and its People count was mostly the same. A person now appears once they have a name of their own, a bio or a picture, and "Just listed" shows listings, not sign-ups. The count of people on the front page follows. Those accounts still work and still open by link.
Search marks the words you typed, not letters inside other words. Searching "lo" marked the middle of "technological"; now only words that start with what you typed are marked, which is how the search matches them.
One keystroke opens one search box. The header carries the search twice (a bar on wide screens, an icon on phones), and each answered ⌘K, so two dialogs opened on top of each other.
Listings made with a test integration key stay off every public list.
A listing with a broken picture shows its initial instead of breaking the page.
Test listings no longer appear on Discover. The first card there was a listing titled "TEST Session — TEST fixture — safe to delete". Listings whose title marks them as tests are now left out of Discover, its counts, search and the sitemap.

Buy a paid ticket without an account. On a paid event, a visitor who isn't signed in types their name and pays in Bitcoin, straight to the organizer's wallet. When the payment lands, the page that opens is the ticket: the QR for the door, the time and place. Close the tab before paying and coming back shows the same request, not a new one. The door list shows them by name; a paid ticket can't be given back from its page, and the organizer refunds it another way and records it, since there is no wallet on record to send Bitcoin back to. {#event-paid-guests}
OrangeCat has one mark now, and it is a cat made of one line. A coil wound inward, two ears on its outer turn — Loki's spiral wearing the cat. It is the same mark in the header, in the browser tab, on the home screen when you install the app, and on every link preview. Until today those were three different drawings, and the tab icon was not an image at all: the file behind it was a web page, so most browsers showed nothing.
The front page opens like a product, not a pricing page. One statement, the mark drawing itself above it, two actions, and real numbers underneath — how many projects are raising, how many people are here, how many studio products are live — counted the same way the directory counts them.
The studio is on the front page. OrangeCat, Loki and Solon with their own faces, and under them every product built on this stack that is live, each one a door to its page. The same list, grouped by layer, now closes the stack page at /ecosystem.
A studio product's own page looks like that product. Loki's project page wears Loki's mark, says it is live, when it last moved, opens its site, and leads to its sibling products.
The front page fits a phone, and a studio product's page opens the product. The line above the headline ran off the right edge of a phone screen; it now shows one phrase there. Loki's page here showed Loki's face but no way to open Loki; it now has the button.
Listing pages open again on phones. Since earlier today, a public product, service or event page with a "Buy" bar at the bottom loaded and then switched to "Something went wrong". The bar asked the browser for something while the page was still being built on the server; it now waits until it reaches the browser.
A seller can no longer hide their own reviews, and a buyer can no longer smuggle words past moderation. Writing to the database directly, a seller could create a back-dated account record that took over their profile and showed an empty track record; a buyer could put arbitrary text where only yes/no answers belong, where hiding the review could not reach it. The server now sets when an account record was created, accepts only the questions OrangeCat asks, and computes each review's and reply's fingerprint itself.
Track records count cancellations. A seller's track record said "N paid deals" including ones later cancelled, without saying so. It now lists cancelled deals next to refunded ones.

Ask your Cat about the people you follow. "What did people I follow post about Lightning this week?" now searches only the people you follow — their public posts and listings, newest first — instead of all of OrangeCat. Nothing they keep private is ever included.
Watch a person, or a topic among the people you follow. Tell your Cat "tell me when @alice posts" (optionally "…about Lightning"), or "tell me when anyone I follow posts about Bitcoin education", and you get a notification for each new public post until you cancel it — never twice for the same post. It works under a post too: "@cat watch her posts for me".

Reviews and track records now show far less about you. Yesterday's version made more public than it should have; this corrects it.
Review reminders respect your email settings. They can be turned off with "Progress & digests" in your notification settings without losing payment receipts, are limited to two emails a day, and several deals waiting at once arrive as one message instead of one each.
A payment OrangeCat sends for you now leaves a record on our side. Until now, money sent from the Send screen or by asking your Cat moved from your wallet and OrangeCat kept no trace that it had. Every send now writes a private record of the payment, the amount and who it went to, and a payment that fails writes one too.

Review the people you buy from and sell to, and only them. Every paid order is now a deal, listed under "Your deals" in the sidebar. Each side can answer a few yes/no questions about the other ("Would you deal with them again?") and add a note. Only the two people in a deal can review it, once each, and a review can never be edited.
You're asked to review, so reviews actually get written. A few days after a deal is paid, each side gets a notification and an email asking how it went, and one more a few days before the review window closes. When the other person reviews you, you hear about it at once (that they reviewed, not what they said). Your Cat's suggestions on the dashboard now include the deal most in need of your review.
Profiles show a track record. A profile now shows what OrangeCat itself saw: how many paid deals the person had, with how many different people, how many were refunded, and what share of the reviews about them say "would deal again". The counts come from settled payments nobody typed in. A profile with no deals shows nothing new.

Explain a transaction by telling your Cat what it was for. Say "the 0.002 that came in on Tuesday was the laptop for Amina" and the Cat, after you confirm, saves it as your note on that transaction. If the wallet publishes its ledger, the note appears there publicly, and it counts toward the wallet's transparency score. Ask the Cat about your wallets and it now lists the recent transactions that still have no note, and the score as the ledger page computes it.
A fund's page shows where to check where its money went. When a cause, research or project page's receiving wallet is fully public and publishes its ledger, the page now says "This fund publishes its ledger" and links to it: every transaction, read from the chain, with the owner's note on what each was for. Funds that have not opted in show nothing new.
A project owner can see their project wallet's transactions. The transaction history checked only who created the wallet row, so the owner of a project wallet could be refused their own history. It now uses the same owner check as every other wallet action.

Every FAQ answer has its own link. Open a question on /faq and share the address: /faq#is-orangecat-free-to-use opens straight at that answer. The page no longer needs its scripts to open a question, and search engines now read the questions and answers directly.
Signing in from Solon or Loki looks like it. The sign-in screen now says "Continue to Solon" beside the form, explains that it is one account with one password, and its back link returns you to the app you came from instead of OrangeCat's home page.
Signing in to Solon and Loki with an email you added later. If you added or changed your email after creating your account (including an account you started without one), OrangeCat told the other app you had no email, and Solon turned you away. It now sends the email your account has.

Sign in without a password. On the sign-in screen, choose "Email me a sign-in code instead": type your email, get a six-digit code, enter it. New here? The same code creates your account. Solon's sign-in uses it too, and so does Loki's "Sign in with OrangeCat".
What you can do here, on one page. Every thing this place can do, in plain words, with an example, the three steps, and a Start button — at /what-you-can-do, from the sidebar, the footer, the create page and How it works.
Say where your public money should go. Of the money you owe the public, how would you divide it between your locality, your region and your nation? Nobody asks. Now you can say it — and see what the people of your place would choose.
New essay: Where the Wall Is. One Hetzner box runs the whole studio today. The piece gives the order in which it stops being enough, what fixes each wall, and why the only one that costs real money is tokens, not servers.
Organisations know what kind of body they are, and where. The kinds of collective — circle, family, association, cooperative, collective, company, guild, DAO, town, network state, local fund — are now one list shared with Solon, and an organisation can say where it belongs (country, region, locality) and what it legally is.
A shorter sidebar, one page for your things, a door on Home. The sidebar had fifteen kinds of thing behind four chevrons. Now it has six lines. Everything you made or joined is one page, My things, and Home starts with a box: say what you want and your Cat drafts it.
Roadmap and changelog now come from the fleet's canonical record. ROADMAP.md and CHANGELOG.md at the repository root are the record; the fleet map ingests them and /roadmap and /changelog render what the map holds. The local copies the pages used to read are gone.

Bring a Claude key straight to Cat. Anthropic is now wired directly, so a Claude key works on its own instead of having to go through OpenRouter. Getting a key from any provider is one click. And there is finally one page explaining what actually powers Cat.
Cat keeps more of your conversation. Cat's instructions are larger than the free tier allows in one go, so some are trimmed on every message. It was trimming your conversation before the generic advice. Now it is the other way round.
Cat keeps its footing when the free tier runs short. When Cat's instructions do not fit the free tier, some are trimmed. Two of the ones it trimmed early were the ones telling it how to answer someone having a hard time. Those are now the last things it will ever give up.
Cat on a phone, fixed end to end. A pass over every screen of Cat and AI settings on a small screen. The box you type in stayed put, replies stopped showing their own formatting marks, and the navigation bar stopped being see-through.
Prices are real; the checkout is deliberately shut. You can now read exactly what Cat costs on every route. You cannot pay us yet, on purpose: OrangeCat is not a registered company, so it must not take money. Paying other people was never affected.

projects.name: solon
projects.what: Governance any group can use — one-click proposals and votes for anyone with an account (Solon's own, or OrangeCat's), Bitcoin signatures for anyone who wants a vote others can recount without trusting Solon, versioned policies and an append-only audit trail.

identity.problem: Lack of transparency and security in traditional governance and treasury management systems
identity.solution: Solon provides a blockchain-based platform for transparent and secure governance and treasury management, using cryptographic methods and Bitcoin-native technology
identity.mission: Solon aims to provide verifiable governance, replacing trust with math and enabling transparent decision-making and treasury management.
identity.vision: Solon envisions a future where governance is transparent, auditable, and secure, using blockchain technology and cryptographic methods.

Cantonal text. A first pass reads each act's document, cut into articles, dated by the day it was read. Zürich now has a reader on the canton's own publication with the canton's in-force date; the other 25 cantons need theirs. The production loads are not done {#law-cantons}
Acts can be found and read on Solon itself, with the publisher's link, the page each copy was read from and its hash {#law-reading}

Ask the law: a chat that plans which places and law words a question needs, searches those provisions and answers from them only, citing each one; public, in any language {#law-ask}
Earlier versions of every act, and what changed between them {#law-history}
